en: Then, the unfailing power of Śiva, the god of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor—power that is all-gracious and full of strength—[manifested]. || 1 ||
By the will of Śiva, she exists as both one and many;
as Vidyā, Vidyeśvarī, and Īśānī, she shines forth in the state that has existed from the beginning of time.
Empowered by that [energy] and possessing sovereign power over all,
the Vidyeśvaras, beginning with Ananteśa, came into being through the will of the Cause.
Other than them are those of immeasurable power, and other than them are the appointed officials;
they are pure-souled beings who bestow white and black fruits.
From them also arose others who possessed passion and were subject to the will of their lords, from whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings was produced. (5)
Mantras, born from the power of the Lord and possessing unfailing potency,
act solely by the will of Śiva throughout the vast path that culminates in Śiva.

The "path" (adhvan) here refers to the road to be traversed; that does not exist for the Lord (pati), nor is it sung of the individual soul (yātṛ-puṃs), because both of these possess omnipresence (vibhutva). || 7 ||
If there were omnipresence, then there would be movement; but omnipresence cannot logically coexist with movement.
Since, in reality, time does not exist as a substance, how could those two [space and time] possibly exist? (8)
When this matter had been thus questioned, O best of the twice-born,
the Lord, the Sovereign of the Lords of the World, spoke with a profound voice.
O Brahman, although both possess omnipresence, just as there is a most extensive path between them, so too is the movement of the Puruṣa described; listen.

Since the ritual of initiation (dīkṣākarma) has been described in sequence as occurring within the transformation of Māyā, that path is therefore a transformation consisting of a specific spatial progression. || 11 ||
Having attained the state of being bound to a husband, she may, by the will of her husband,
gradually be led away from her course toward Śiva for the sake of his welfare.
That which is more internal is to be purified, as is that which is more external;
once the external has been removed, the sequence of internal activity occurs.
Thus has the path of Śiva been described according to the logic of the sequence of ascent;
and in the world, this arrangement of the path is observed to be based upon real entities.
That which is the final state of a person whose seed of saṃsāra has been burnt should be understood as his "goal" (gati); it is not a residence in another location. 15.
Just as in the world, when one property is manifested through another property, an object such as a cloth or a leaf is spoken of [in that way], so too is the person (puruṣa). 16.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the Power of Grace, in the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha.
